messages.content: I want to develop tactile slip prediction that distinguishes impending grasp slip from elastic deformation, including when the material is unseen or the tactile sensor is worn. The prediction needs to come at least 100 milliseconds before slip, with at least 90% recall and no more than a 5% false-positive rate. Those targets also need to hold on held-out materials and worn sensors, including deformation-only contacts matched for force.

The goal has two parts that need to be satisfied together. The predictor must anticipate grasp slip at least 100 milliseconds ahead, while avoiding the mistake of treating elastic deformation as impending slip. At that lead time, the targets are ≥90% recall and ≤5% false-positive rate. The same targets apply under the stated evaluation conditions: held-out materials and worn sensors, with force-matched deformation-only contacts included among the cases that should not be called slip.
Why is the distinction between impending slip and elastic deformation central rather than just a separate accuracy detail?

Because a positive prediction is meant to indicate that slip is impending, not merely that the tactile contact is changing. Elastic deformation can be a change in contact without being grasp slip. If deformation-only contacts are frequently labeled as impending slip, the system would fail the distinction even if it identified many actual slip cases. The false-positive limit therefore matters alongside recall, not as an afterthought.
So the 90% figure is not saying that 90% of all predictions should be correct?

Right. Recall refers to the share of actual slip cases that receive a slip prediction meeting the required lead time. The requirement is at least 90% recall. It is not, by itself, an overall accuracy figure, and it does not say how often a slip prediction is correct. The separate false-positive-rate requirement limits mistaken slip predictions on cases where slip is not impending.
And how should I read the 5% false-positive ceiling here?

It means false slip indications must remain at or below a 5% false-positive rate. Deformation-only contacts are particularly relevant to that ceiling because they test whether the predictor mistakes elastic deformation for impending slip. The goal does not specify a particular counting unit for that rate, so I would preserve the stated threshold without assuming an event-level or sample-level scoring convention.
Does a correct warning right when slip begins satisfy the timing requirement?

No. The requested prediction is at least 100 milliseconds ahead of slip. A signal that first identifies slip at its onset would not establish that advance prediction, even if it identifies the event correctly. The timing requirement and the recall requirement have to be read together: the slip cases counted as successfully predicted need a qualifying early prediction.
What does matching the deformation-only contacts for force add to the evaluation?

It makes the deformation-only contacts a more pointed test of the intended distinction. If those contacts are matched for force, a difference in force alone should not be treated as the explanation for separating them from the slip cases. The stated objective remains to distinguish impending grasp slip from elastic deformation while keeping false positives within the limit. The goal does not specify a force-matching procedure, so it would be premature to assume one.
Could we satisfy the requirement by performing well on familiar materials, then report the worn-sensor and unseen-material cases separately without holding them to the same numbers?

That would not express the stated requirement. The targets—prediction at least 100 milliseconds ahead, ≥90% recall, and ≤5% false-positive rate—need to be met on held-out materials and worn sensors as well. Performance on familiar conditions alone would not establish that the goal has been met.
When you say held-out materials, are you claiming anything specific about which materials they are?

No. “Held-out materials” identifies the generalization condition, but the goal does not name the materials or specify how many there are. Likewise, it calls for performance with worn sensors without specifying a degree of wear. Those details should not be filled in as though they were already given.
I also don't want “unseen materials and sensor wear” to turn into a vague promise of robustness. What remains measurable?

The measurable requirements remain explicit: slip prediction at least 100 milliseconds ahead, with recall of at least 90% and a false-positive rate of no more than 5%. Those targets must be met on held-out materials and worn sensors, and the evaluation must include deformation-only contacts matched for force. “Robustness” is a shorthand for meeting those stated conditions, not a substitute for them.
Suppose someone emphasizes the lead time and recall but barely mentions deformation-only contacts. Would that still capture the goal?

It would leave out an essential part. The goal is not only to anticipate slip; it is to distinguish impending grasp slip from elastic deformation. Force-matched deformation-only contacts make that distinction explicit in the conditions under which the targets must hold. A description focused solely on early slip detections would miss the stated concern about false slip indications.
Conversely, if it rejects deformation-only contacts well but detects slip too late, is that enough?

No. Avoiding false positives cannot replace the requirement to anticipate actual slip. Both sides matter: at least 90% recall for slip predictions made at least 100 milliseconds ahead, and at most a 5% false-positive rate. The intended performance must also carry over to the specified held-out-material and worn-sensor conditions.
I want to be careful not to present any of this as an achieved result.

That is the right distinction in wording. This is a development goal with performance requirements, not a report that a predictor has already met them. It is accurate to say the predictor should distinguish impending grasp slip from elastic deformation and should meet the numerical targets under the stated conditions; it would not be accurate to claim success without results.
Is there anything else in the wording that should stay precise?

Keep “at least 100 milliseconds ahead” attached to predicting slip, rather than weakening it to detecting slip quickly. Keep ≥90% recall distinct from ≤5% false-positive rate. And retain all of the conditions: held-out materials, worn sensors, and deformation-only contacts matched for force. None of those conditions is interchangeable with a general claim of good performance.

For the tactile slip goal, I propose training a wear-augmented, material-adversarial shear-field encoder to forecast slip 100 milliseconds ahead from microslip, using force-matched elastic contacts as negatives. Can you unpack that without treating it as an established result?

Yes. This is a proposed training approach, not evidence that the targets have been met. The encoder would use tactile shear-field information associated with microslip to make a prediction 100 milliseconds ahead. Wear augmentation is intended to address variation from sensor wear, while material-adversarial training is intended to discourage dependence on features specific to the training materials. Force-matched elastic contacts serve as negative examples so the model must distinguish impending slip from elastic deformation rather than respond to force alone.
When you say it forecasts slip from microslip, are you saying microslip and grasp slip are the same event?

No. In the proposal, microslip is information used to forecast impending grasp slip; it is not being equated with the grasp-slip event being predicted. The useful distinction is between a cue available before the event and the event the predictor is meant to anticipate. Whether those cues actually support a reliable 100-millisecond forecast remains to be tested.
What does the shear-field encoder contribute to that description?

It names the proposed input representation and learning component: an encoder operating on tactile shear-field information. The proposal does not specify its architecture, the exact shear-field measurements, or a particular way of extracting microslip. Those would be additional design choices, not facts already established by this proposal.
Why include wear augmentation rather than only evaluating on worn sensors at the end?

Wear augmentation is the training-side part of the proposal: it aims to expose the encoder to variation associated with sensor wear. Evaluation on worn sensors is still a separate question. Training with augmentation would not, by itself, demonstrate that performance on worn sensors meets the required recall, false-positive rate, or lead time.
And does material-adversarial mean the encoder can no longer use any information that happens to differ between materials?

That would be too strong a claim. The proposed material-adversarial aspect is intended to reduce reliance on material-specific cues so the forecast can transfer to unseen materials. It does not guarantee that the learned representation is independent of material, nor does the proposal specify exactly how that adversarial objective would be implemented.
I want the force-matched elastic negatives to be more than a passing mention. What role do they play in training?

They are the proposed negative examples against which impending-slip examples are contrasted. They represent elastic contacts without slip, matched for force, so a model cannot be considered to have learned the intended distinction merely because it reacts differently to different force levels. The point is to train toward recognizing slip-relevant information in the shear field without treating deformation alone as a positive prediction.
Does that imply every elastic contact is force matched, or that a particular matching rule has been chosen?

No. The proposal says to use force-matched elastic negatives, but it does not define a matching rule or describe how many contacts would be used. It is important to preserve the force-matched condition without inventing a procedure for satisfying it.
How does the 100-millisecond forecast in this proposal relate to the larger performance targets?

The proposal aims at the required advance warning by forecasting slip 100 milliseconds ahead. The larger goal also requires at least 90% recall and no more than a 5% false-positive rate, including on held-out materials and worn sensors with force-matched deformation-only contacts. The proposed training approach is meant to address those challenges, but it does not itself show that any of those performance thresholds have been reached.
Could the elastic negatives help with recall as well as false positives?

Their clearest stated role is to sharpen the distinction between impending slip and elastic deformation, which is directly relevant to avoiding false slip predictions. Their effect on recall is not specified. A trained model would still need to catch enough actual slip cases at the required lead time; improving rejection of elastic contacts would not automatically establish that.
If someone describes this simply as a wear-resistant slip detector, what would get lost?

That description loses several parts of the proposal: it is a forecast 100 milliseconds ahead, not just detection; it uses a shear-field encoder and microslip as predictive information; it includes material-adversarial training as well as wear augmentation; and it uses force-matched elastic negatives to address confusion with deformation. “Wear-resistant” would also sound like a demonstrated property, whereas here resistance to wear-related variation is an aim of the training proposal.
Would it be fair to call the material-adversarial component an attempt to generalize beyond the training materials?

Yes, as an attempt. The goal includes held-out materials, and the material-adversarial component is proposed to reduce reliance on cues tied to materials seen during training. Generalization to held-out materials still has to be established by performance under that condition; the component's name alone is not proof.
Is there any reason to say that microslip must occur in every eventual slip case for this proposal to make sense?

The proposal does not make that universal claim. It says to forecast slip from microslip, identifying the cue it intends to use. It leaves open whether that cue is available and informative often enough to achieve the required recall at the specified lead time. We should not assume coverage across every eventual slip case.
Can you restate the proposed approach in one sentence while keeping it clearly prospective?

Train a wear-augmented, material-adversarial shear-field encoder that uses microslip information to forecast grasp slip 100 milliseconds ahead, with force-matched elastic contacts as negatives, then assess whether it meets the stated performance targets on held-out materials and worn sensors.

The key question for me is whether wear-attenuated shear precursors remain separable from force-matched elastic relaxation 100 milliseconds before slip on unseen materials. How should I interpret that question?

It asks whether the shear information available 100 milliseconds before an actual grasp slip still distinguishes impending slip from elastic relaxation when sensor wear attenuates the precursors and the material was not seen during training. The elastic-relaxation contacts are matched for force, so the distinction cannot simply rest on a difference in force. It is an open question about the available signal, not a claim that the distinction has already been demonstrated.
What does “remain separable” mean here? Does it imply the two kinds of contact must never look alike?

No. It asks whether there is enough distinguishing information for a useful forecast under those conditions. It does not assert perfect separation, or that every example of impending slip looks unlike every example of elastic relaxation. Nor does the wording specify a particular measure of separability. The concern is whether a predictor can tell the two apart early enough without routinely calling relaxation slip.
Why emphasize wear attenuation instead of simply saying the sensor is worn?

“Wear-attenuated shear precursors” focuses the question on what happens if wear weakens the prospective shear cues. The question is whether any useful distinction survives that attenuation at the required time. It does not specify the degree of attenuation or establish that the cues disappear; those should not be assumed.
Is the question asking whether elastic relaxation itself becomes more likely after wear?

No. It asks whether the shear precursors of impending slip, as available through a worn sensor, can be distinguished from force-matched elastic relaxation. It does not make a claim about wear changing the frequency or physical character of elastic relaxation.
What exactly is being compared at the 100-millisecond point?

On the slip side, the question concerns information available 100 milliseconds before slip occurs. On the negative side, it concerns force-matched elastic relaxation without the impending slip that the predictor is meant to forecast. The wording does not define a particular way to align or sample those negative contacts in time, so it is best not to invent one.
Would a shear pattern visible only once the grasp starts slipping answer the question?

No. Even if it were distinctive, a pattern that only becomes available when slip starts would not establish separability 100 milliseconds beforehand. This question is specifically about prospective information at that lead time, rather than recognition of slip after its onset.
Could a model distinguish the examples by recognizing the material instead?

That would not address the question as posed. It asks about distinguishing the contacts on unseen materials, so a distinction that depends on recognizing particular training materials would not establish the desired separation there. The proposed material-adversarial shear-field encoder is one attempt to address that concern, but the question of whether the relevant cues transfer remains open.
Does force matching mean the elastic relaxation and impending-slip cases have identical tactile signals apart from slip?

No. Force matching constrains the comparison with respect to force; it does not declare every other aspect of the tactile signals identical. Its importance here is that a difference attributed to impending slip should not merely be a difference in force between the slip and elastic-relaxation examples. Whether a distinct shear precursor remains is precisely what the question asks.
I'm trying not to smuggle in the answer by calling them “precursors.” Does that word already prove they predict slip?

Not in this context. “Shear precursors” identifies candidate information preceding slip, especially the microslip-related information considered in the proposed approach. Calling it a precursor does not establish that it is reliably distinguishable from elastic relaxation, that it survives wear attenuation, or that it transfers to unseen materials at the 100-millisecond lead time.
If the signals are separable on familiar materials, does that settle the unseen-material part?

No. Separation on familiar materials would not, by itself, answer whether it persists on unseen materials. The unseen-material condition is part of the question, not an optional extension of it. The same caution applies to the wear-attenuated condition: an apparent distinction without that condition would not resolve the question as worded.
Could “separable” just mean that a few especially clear slip cases look different from elastic relaxation?

A few clear cases would show that a difference can sometimes be visible, but they would not establish that the distinction is useful across the specified conditions. The broader goal requires catching impending slip while limiting false slip indications. This question probes whether the candidate signal can support that distinction at 100 milliseconds before slip, on unseen materials and with wear attenuation, rather than only in especially clear examples.
How does this relate to the wear-augmented encoder proposal without assuming that training strategy works?

The proposal would train a shear-field encoder using wear augmentation and force-matched elastic negatives, with a material-adversarial component aimed at transfer across materials. This question probes a premise relevant to that approach: whether the early, wear-attenuated shear information remains distinguishable from the negative contacts on unseen materials at all. Naming a training strategy does not answer the signal-level question.
Could wear augmentation create a distinction if no distinguishable information remains in the worn-sensor signal?

The question does not establish whether information remains, so it is important to keep that conditional. A training method can aim to use information that is present despite wear; it should not be assumed to recover a distinction that is absent from the available signal. Whether there is enough information is what this question leaves unresolved.
What if the elastic relaxation also produces changing shear information?

That possibility is exactly why the comparison matters. A changing shear field alone should not be presumed to indicate impending grasp slip. The question asks whether the prospective, wear-attenuated shear cues of slip can be distinguished from force-matched elastic relaxation, rather than treating any tactile change as a warning.
So is this primarily a question about recall or about false positives?

It bears on both, without supplying either result. If the early slip cues cannot be recognized, slip predictions could be missed; if elastic relaxation is mistaken for those cues, false slip predictions could follow. The question is narrower than a performance claim: it asks whether the underlying distinction remains available 100 milliseconds ahead under wear attenuation and on unseen materials.
Can I phrase the uncertainty directly, without suggesting that worn sensors or unseen materials necessarily destroy the signal?

Yes: “It remains to be determined whether shear precursors attenuated by sensor wear can still be distinguished from force-matched elastic relaxation 100 milliseconds before grasp slip on unseen materials.” That states the comparison and conditions while leaving the answer open.

I want to state the hypothesis plainly: shear residuals distinguish slip 100 milliseconds ahead from force-matched elastic relaxation on unseen materials and worn sensors, at ≥90% recall and ≤5% false-positive rate. Is that a fair statement of what we're testing?

Yes, as a hypothesis rather than a finding. It proposes that shear residuals contain enough information to predict impending slip at least 100 milliseconds before it occurs while distinguishing it from force-matched elastic relaxation. The proposed distinction must achieve at least 90% recall and no more than a 5% false-positive rate under the stated unseen-material and worn-sensor conditions.
I don't want the word “distinguish” to sound like perfect separation. Does the hypothesis require that?

No. Its numerical thresholds make the intended claim more precise than perfect separation: ≥90% recall and ≤5% false-positive rate. Some misses or false indications could still occur within those limits. The hypothesis is that the distinction is strong enough to meet both thresholds at the specified lead time and under the specified conditions.
What should we mean by “shear residuals” here? Have we specified how to compute them?

The hypothesis names shear residuals as the candidate distinguishing information, but it does not specify a calculation or a reference against which the residual is taken. We can discuss their proposed role without claiming a particular computation has been selected. Defining the residual precisely would require information beyond this statement.
Is the hypothesis that residuals distinguish materials from one another, or that they distinguish slip from relaxation?

The distinction at issue is impending slip versus force-matched elastic relaxation. Unseen materials are a condition under which that distinction is hypothesized to hold, not the classes the residuals are supposed to identify.
Likewise, do worn sensors count as a category to classify?
No. Worn sensors are another condition under which the hypothesized slip-versus-relaxation distinction must hold. The claim is not that shear residuals identify whether a sensor is worn.
How tightly does the 100-millisecond requirement attach to the recall figure?

It attaches directly. The hypothesis concerns slip predicted at least 100 milliseconds ahead, with ≥90% recall. Counting predictions that first appear at slip onset would change the claim: they would not satisfy the stated advance-warning requirement.
If elastic relaxation produces a false slip warning, where does that appear in these numbers?

It is relevant to the false-positive rate. The hypothesis requires ≤5% FPR while distinguishing impending slip from force-matched elastic relaxation. That ceiling prevents high recall from standing alone as evidence for the proposed distinction if relaxation is often mistaken for slip.
Why keep “force-matched” in the hypothesis rather than just say “elastic relaxation”?

Because it specifies a more demanding comparison. The elastic-relaxation contacts are matched for force to the slip comparison, so success cannot be described merely as responding differently to an obvious force difference. The hypothesis is about a distinguishable slip-related signal in the shear residuals under that comparison; it does not say that force matching makes all other contact properties identical.
Could I claim the numbers if they held on unseen materials but not on worn sensors?

Not as this hypothesis is written. It includes both unseen materials and worn sensors among the conditions where the ≥90% recall and ≤5% FPR distinction is proposed to hold. Meeting the numbers under only one of those conditions would not establish the whole claim.
Does the wording tell us exactly how unseen materials and worn sensors must be combined in individual cases?

No. It names both conditions, but it does not prescribe a particular grouping, sampling scheme, or breakdown of the evaluation. We should preserve both conditions without inventing a more detailed testing arrangement.
Is this hypothesis stronger than merely saying there might be some difference between early slip and elastic relaxation?

Yes. It predicts a distinction that is useful at a specified time and to specified performance levels: at least 100 milliseconds ahead, ≥90% recall, and ≤5% FPR, on unseen materials and worn sensors. A slight difference that cannot support those thresholds would not be enough for the hypothesis as stated.
Would observing distinctive shear residuals after slip begins bear directly on it?

It would not establish the central timing claim. This hypothesis concerns the information available for a forecast 100 milliseconds before slip. Residuals that only become distinctive afterward could not by themselves support the proposed advance prediction.
Do we have to assume that the proposed shear-field encoder has already learned to use the residuals?

No. The hypothesis is about whether shear residuals can support the stated distinction and performance. The proposed encoder is one possible approach to making the forecast, but neither its training nor its success is established by stating this hypothesis.
I want to avoid implying that wear has no effect at all. Is that implication present?

No. The hypothesis says the distinction remains strong enough to meet the thresholds on worn sensors; it does not say that worn-sensor signals are identical to unworn ones or that wear has no effect. Whether the hypothesized performance actually persists must still be determined.
And “≥90% recall, ≤5% FPR” should not be compressed into a single accuracy number, correct?

Correct. Recall concerns how many impending slips receive a qualifying early prediction; false-positive rate concerns mistaken slip indications on negatives such as force-matched elastic relaxation. They constrain different kinds of errors, and the hypothesis specifies both. It does not supply an overall accuracy figure.
Can you give me a cautious version that keeps the quantitative claim intact?

We hypothesize that shear residuals can distinguish impending grasp slip at least 100 milliseconds before onset from force-matched elastic relaxation on unseen materials and worn sensors, achieving ≥90% recall with ≤5% false-positive rate. This states what is proposed without implying that the thresholds have already been demonstrated.

For the open question about early shear cues, the plan is to collect WearSlip-12 force-matched deformation and slip trials, train the wear-augmented encoder, and then measure 100-millisecond recall and false-positive rate on held-out materials and sensors. Can you walk through what that plan does and does not establish?

It sets out a sequence, not a result. First, collect WearSlip-12 trials that include deformation and slip contacts matched for force. Next, train the wear-augmented encoder. Then measure recall for slip predictions 100 milliseconds ahead and the false-positive rate on held-out materials and sensors. Those measurements would bear on whether the early distinction holds beyond the training conditions, but the plan does not yet say what the measurements will be.
What is the purpose of including deformation trials rather than collecting only slip trials?

The task is to distinguish impending slip from deformation, not simply to recognize a pattern that appears before slip. Deformation trials provide contacts that should not be treated as impending slip. Matching them for force makes that comparison more focused: a predictor should not appear successful merely because the slip and deformation contacts differ in force.
Does the plan say how force matching will be done?
No. It specifies force-matched deformation and slip trials, but it does not give a matching criterion or procedure. Those details cannot be inferred from the plan.
Should we describe WearSlip-12 as twelve materials or twelve sensors?

No. WearSlip-12 is the name given for the planned trial collection. The plan does not explain what the “12” denotes, so assigning it to a number of materials, sensors, or anything else would add an unsupported fact.
How important is the order of collecting trials, training, and measuring performance?

It is explicit in the plan: collect the force-matched trials, train the wear-augmented encoder, then measure 100-millisecond recall and false-positive rate on held-out materials and sensors. Describing the measurements as already completed, or treating the plan as performance evidence, would change its meaning.
What exactly are we measuring with “100-millisecond recall”?

Recall for slip predictions made at the specified advance point: whether actual slip cases receive a prediction 100 milliseconds before slip. The wording does not define the full scoring procedure, so it is best to retain that timing and the recall measure without inventing details about how trials or predictions are counted.
Why measure false-positive rate as well?

Because a predictor that warns on nearly every changing contact might catch many slips while also mistaking deformation for slip. False-positive rate measures that other side of the distinction. The force-matched deformation trials make mistaken warnings on elastic contacts particularly relevant to the question the plan is meant to examine.
Does the plan itself say the encoder will reach ≥90% recall and ≤5% false-positive rate?

No. Those are the performance targets of the broader goal, not outcomes established by this plan. The plan says to measure 100-millisecond recall and false-positive rate after training, on held-out materials and sensors. Only the resulting measurements could show whether the targets are met.
If I call this a test of generalization, what is the precise basis for that wording?

The planned measurements are on held-out materials and sensors rather than only on conditions used for training. That is why the evaluation bears on transfer beyond the training conditions. The plan does not specify which materials or sensors are held out, how many there are, or how the holdout is arranged.
The larger goal mentions worn sensors. Does “held-out sensors” tell us exactly what wear conditions are in the evaluation?

No. The plan calls for a wear-augmented encoder and evaluation on held-out sensors, but it does not specify the wear condition of those sensors or how wear is represented in the trials. The larger goal's worn-sensor requirement remains relevant, yet this plan should not be paraphrased as specifying a particular worn-sensor evaluation that it does not describe.
Likewise, does “wear-augmented encoder” tell us how augmentation is generated?

No. It identifies the encoder to be trained as wear-augmented, without specifying an augmentation technique or the amount of wear it is intended to represent. The phrase describes a planned training component, not an implemented procedure or proof of robustness.
Would this plan answer whether shear precursors are separable from elastic relaxation by simply observing the training performance?

Training performance alone is not the measurement this plan identifies for that purpose. It calls for measuring 100-millisecond recall and false-positive rate on held-out materials and sensors after training. Those outcomes would be more directly relevant to whether the proposed distinction persists under the stated holdout conditions, without assuming in advance that it does.
Can I say the trials are deformation-only contacts matched for force against slip trials?

You can describe the planned negative side as force-matched deformation trials in the context of distinguishing deformation from slip. That preserves the intended comparison. Avoid adding an unprovided trial protocol or implying that matching force makes the two kinds of contact identical in every other respect.
What does this plan leave unanswered even after I've stated it clearly?

It leaves the outcome unanswered: whether the trained encoder will actually distinguish impending slip from force-matched deformation 100 milliseconds ahead, and what recall and false-positive rate it will achieve on held-out materials and sensors. It also leaves implementation and evaluation details unspecified, including the force-matching procedure, the augmentation method, and the makeup of the held-out sets. None of those omissions should be filled with assumed facts.
Give me a concise prospective statement that keeps the dataset name, order, and evaluation conditions.

We plan to collect WearSlip-12 force-matched deformation and slip trials, train the wear-augmented encoder, and then measure 100-millisecond recall and false-positive rate on held-out materials and sensors. This is a planned test of the early slip-versus-deformation distinction, not a claim that the performance targets have been met.

The evaluation activity is to test the wear-augmented encoder on WearSlip-12’s held-out materials and worn sensors, measuring 100-millisecond recall and false-positive rate on force-matched deformation contacts. What should that description convey?

It identifies both the evaluation conditions and the two measurements. The encoder is evaluated on held-out materials and worn sensors. Recall concerns slip predictions made 100 milliseconds ahead; the false-positive rate concerns mistaken slip predictions on force-matched deformation contacts. The description specifies what to measure, not what the results are.
Is this just an evaluation of whether the encoder recognizes slip at some point?

No. The timing is essential: the recall measurement is for predictions 100 milliseconds before slip, not simply recognition once slip has begun. The deformation false-positive measurement checks the other side of the task—whether contacts without impending slip are incorrectly flagged.
Why name both held-out materials and worn sensors?

They identify conditions under which the encoder is to be evaluated. Held-out materials probe performance beyond the materials used for training, and worn sensors probe performance when the sensor is worn. Neither condition should disappear into a general statement that the encoder is being tested for robustness.
Does a wear-augmented encoder automatically count as evaluated on worn sensors?

No. “Wear-augmented” describes the encoder, while evaluation on worn sensors is a separate part of this activity. The training description alone does not supply a worn-sensor result; the specified evaluation is what would measure performance under that condition.
Could we report only the 100-millisecond recall and leave deformation contacts out of the evaluation description?

That would omit an explicit measurement. This activity calls for the false-positive rate on force-matched deformation contacts as well as 100-millisecond recall. High recall alone would not tell us whether the encoder confuses deformation with impending slip.
What makes the deformation false-positive rate more specific than a generic false-positive rate?

It names the negative contacts of interest: deformation contacts matched for force. The measurement therefore focuses on false slip indications in a comparison where force alone is not meant to distinguish the contacts. The activity does not specify a force-matching method or a scoring convention beyond that description.
Does force matching mean the deformation contacts must have identical shear fields to the slip contacts?

No. It specifies matching with respect to force, not identity of the complete tactile signal. The evaluation asks whether the encoder can avoid calling those deformation contacts slip while still predicting actual slip early enough.
When we say “100-millisecond recall,” should that be understood as recall measured after slip starts but within a 100-millisecond window?

No. Here it refers to forecasting slip 100 milliseconds ahead. Recasting it as a window after onset would reverse the timing of the activity. The description does not, however, give further details of how predictions are scored.
Are the held-out materials and worn sensors necessarily the same set of trials, or two separate slices?

The activity names both evaluation conditions but does not specify their grouping. It would be an added detail to assert either a particular combined set or a particular separate breakdown. We can state that evaluation covers held-out materials and worn sensors without inventing how the trials are partitioned.
Does WearSlip-12 tell us how many held-out materials or worn sensors there are?
No. WearSlip-12 is the named source for this evaluation, but the activity does not specify counts of materials or sensors. The name alone should not be interpreted as a count or an evaluation design.
Would it be accurate to write that this evaluation verifies the hypothesis about early shear information?

It is more careful to say that the evaluation tests it. Measuring early recall and deformation false positives under the held-out-material and worn-sensor conditions bears on the proposed distinction. Without the measurements, the activity does not establish whether that distinction succeeds.
What if someone describes the outcome as meeting the target simply because these are the metrics being measured?

That would confuse a measurement specification with a result. This activity says to measure 100-millisecond recall and force-matched deformation false-positive rate; it supplies no values for either. Whether any performance target is met remains an outcome of the evaluation, not a premise of it.
Could I call the false-positive measurement a test of elastic relaxation specifically?

You can connect it to the slip-versus-elastic-deformation question, but keep the activity’s wording precise: it measures false-positive rate on force-matched deformation contacts. Calling those contacts a more narrowly defined subtype, or claiming a particular relaxation procedure, would add detail that the activity does not provide.
What distinction should a reader keep in mind between the two measurements?

Recall asks how often actual slips receive a qualifying prediction 100 milliseconds ahead. The force-matched deformation false-positive rate asks how often deformation contacts are incorrectly treated as impending slip. They address different failure modes, so neither measurement can stand in for the other.
Can you put the activity in one prospective sentence without implying the evaluation has produced findings?

Evaluate the wear-augmented encoder on WearSlip-12’s held-out materials and worn sensors, measuring recall for slip forecast 100 milliseconds ahead and the false-positive rate on force-matched deformation contacts.

We now have the WearSlip-12 evaluation figures: on held-out materials and worn sensors, 100-millisecond recall reached 92%, but the false-positive rate on force-matched deformation contacts was 13%. How should I state that accurately?

State both results and keep their scopes distinct: “On WearSlip-12 held-out materials and worn sensors, recall for slip predicted 100 milliseconds ahead was 92%, while the false-positive rate on force-matched deformation contacts was 13%.” The first figure describes early predictions of actual slip; the second describes mistaken slip indications on the specified deformation negatives.
Does “100-millisecond recall” mean the encoder recognized slip within 100 milliseconds after it started?
No. The timing here is prospective: the recall figure concerns prediction 100 milliseconds before slip. Describing it as recognition after onset would change what the 92% measures.
I used “but” between the two numbers. Is that contrast justified?

Yes, as a contrast between detecting impending slip and avoiding mistaken warnings on deformation. The 92% recall shows how often the evaluation registered a qualifying early slip prediction; the 13% false-positive rate shows that force-matched deformation still drew mistaken slip indications. “But” need not imply a known cause for either result.
Can I call 13% the false-positive rate for every kind of non-slip contact?
No. The reported 13% is specifically the false-positive rate on force-matched deformation contacts. The evidence does not give a false-positive rate across all possible non-slip contacts.
Does force matching mean those contacts were otherwise indistinguishable from the slip contacts?
